column4: Israel's exchange asks, أَتَسْتَبْدِلُونَ ٱلَّذِى هُوَ أَدْنَىٰ بِٱلَّذِى هُوَ خَيْرٌ, staging the section's condemned choice of the lower for the better.
Floodwater and molten ore cast up foam that vanishes as refuse, while what benefits people remains on earth; this is the section's sorting of dross from the abiding good in a single image.
The threatened magicians say لَن نُّؤْثِرَكَ over the proofs and their Creator, reversing 87:16's censured preference while limiting Pharaoh's power to this worldly life.
The magicians conclude وَٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ; the exact better-and-more-lasting pair names what their refusal in 20:72 selects.
وَءَاثَرَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا is the section's wrong preference verb and object repeated exactly in the Pharaoh passage.
Hell becoming the wrong chooser's shelter supplies the consequence of 79:38 and one side of the section's openly staged selection.
Fear of standing before the Lord and restraining the self from desire enact the opposite choice to preferring the lower life.
Paradise becoming the shelter completes 79:40 and the two-outcome sorting begun by 79:38-39.
The worldly display is a flower not to be stared at, while وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ joins the pasture image to better, lasting provision.
Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment and adornment, whereas وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ states the section's valuation exactly.
Worldly gifts are enjoyment of this life, while وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ identifies the believers' better, enduring share.
The command not to sell God's covenant for a small price says what is with God is better, making a concrete act of the choice whose durability 16:96 explains.
مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍ draws the section's exact line between what runs out and what remains.
The likeness of worldly life becomes rain-grown vegetation and then wind-scattered stubble, joining the lower life directly to the pasture's discarded residue.
After naming wealth and children as worldly adornment, the ayah calls ٱلْبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ better with the Lord, the good remainder opposite 18:45's stubble.
Worldly life is compared to rain-grown plants that yellow and become debris before the ayah sets punishment, forgiveness, and divine approval beyond them.
كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ states the passing side of the section's division without metaphorical extension.
وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ gives the surviving side and supports the dictionary claim that God alone possesses unconditioned permanence.
كَلَّا بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ rebukes the same collective attachment as 87:16, calling its object the immediate life.
وَتَذَرُونَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ makes explicit that loving the immediate means leaving the lasting counterpart unchosen.
إِنَّ هَٰؤُلَآءِ يُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ وَيَذَرُونَ وَرَآءَهُمْ يَوْمًا ثَقِيلًا restages choosing the near life and casting the consequential day behind.
Those who يَسْتَحِبُّونَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا عَلَى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ enact the same preference even with a different verb.
Punishment is traced to their having preferred worldly life over the hereafter, an explicit causal version of the section's rebuke.
The question أَرَضِيتُم بِٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا مِنَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ confronts the addressees' choice and answers that worldly enjoyment is little by comparison.
Those who bought worldly life at the price of the hereafter turn preference into an exchange whose consequence cannot be reduced or relieved.
The answer to people clinging to worldly delay says its enjoyment is little and the hereafter is better for the God-fearing.
تُرِيدُونَ عَرَضَ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱللَّهُ يُرِيدُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ sets human desire for immediate captive-gain against God's desired horizon.
The ayah places the seeker of worldly reward and the seeker of otherworldly reward in parallel clauses, making the selection and its apportioned result explicit.
مِنكُم مَّن يُرِيدُ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَمِنكُم مَّن يُرِيدُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ identifies the battlefield split as two differently chosen ends.
Whoever desires worldly life and its adornment receives the full return of deeds there, defining the apparently favored portion before its loss is exposed.
The same choosers have only the Fire in the hereafter and their work becomes void, so what looked selected proves to be refuse.
Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God wills and is then assigned hell, directly staging the lower choice and its end.
Whoever wants the hereafter, strives for it, and believes has an appreciated striving, the positive side of 17:18's selection.
God supplies both groups from His bounty, clarifying that the difference lies in what each chooses rather than an unavailable worldly provision.
Worldly gradations are followed by the declaration that the hereafter is greater in rank and preference, correcting the scale by which people select.
The Prophet's wives are offered a literal choice: worldly life and adornment with an honorable release.
Choosing God, His Messenger, and the final home instead brings the good-doers a great reward, completing the two-sided offer of 33:28.
The cultivator of the hereafter has that harvest increased, while the cultivator of the world gets some of it but no otherworldly share; the agricultural image makes selection yield its own crop.
The person whose prayer asks only for this world is said to have no share in the hereafter, one side of a paired choice.
The answering prayer seeks good in both world and hereafter, setting a right ordering that does not call every worldly good refuse.
أُولَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمْ نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا assigns the correctly ordered seekers a lasting earned portion and completes the pair.
Those desiring worldly life see Qarun's splendor and wish for his portion, a narrated instance of selecting by the lower life's glitter.
People given knowledge answer that God's reward is better for the believer who acts rightly, correcting the spectators' standard of choice.
This life is called temporary enjoyment while the hereafter is دَارُ ٱلْقَرَارِ, the settled abode, directly opposing passing possession to permanence.
Worldly life is play and diversion, while the final abode is called the true life; the ayah reverses the surface judgment of what deserves choosing.
Worldly life is play and diversion, whereas the final abode is better for the God-fearing, stating the same comparative scale.
Successors repeatedly take عَرَضَ هَٰذَا ٱلْأَدْنَىٰ while the final abode is better for the God-fearing, joining the lower object's root to a recurrent bad selection.
After asking readers to observe earlier peoples' ends, the ayah says the final abode is better for the God-fearing.
Those who answer that their Lord sent good receive good here, but the ayah still declares the final abode better, ordering two genuine goods.
وَلَلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لَّكَ مِنَ ٱلْأُولَىٰ gives the Prophet the same better-later valuation in a personal promise.
Loved appetites, accumulated wealth, livestock, and tilled land are gathered as the enjoyment of worldly life, making the attractive lower pan concrete.
قُلْ أَؤُنَبِّئُكُم بِخَيْرٍ مِّن ذَٰلِكُمْ answers the worldly list with gardens, purified spouses, and God's approval, explicitly offering the better selection.
People leave the Messenger standing when they see commerce or amusement, and the ayah answers that what is with God is better than both and that He is the best provider.
Family, acquired wealth, feared commercial loss, and pleasing homes are tested as preferred loves against God, His Messenger, and striving in His way.
Those deceived by worldly life made religion play; God then says He forgets them as they forgot their meeting, joining the lower choice to treatment as discarded.
The person who forgot God's signs is told وَكَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْيَوْمَ تُنسَىٰ, turning chosen neglect into being left forgotten before 20:127 names the more enduring punishment.
إِنَّا نَسِينَٰكُمْ كَمَا نَسِيتُمْ لِقَآءَ يَوْمِكُمْ makes reciprocal forgetting the fate of those who discarded the encounter.
The reason given is that they mocked the signs and worldly life deceived them, explicitly linking 45:34's abandonment to the wrong-valued life.
Mary's wish to have been نَسْيًا مَّنسِيًّا uses the root for a forgotten, discarded thing, exactly the section's secondary refuse sense.
After the blast seizes the wrongdoers, God makes them غُثَآءً; people themselves become the pasture refuse invoked by the section's dictionary sense.
بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ names the lawful remainder left after honest dealing as better, uniting remnant, goodness, and right valuation.
أُو۟لُوا۟ بَقِيَّةٍ are the remnant with enough moral good to forbid corruption, the exact human sense the section cites.
فِيهِنَّ خَيْرَٰتٌ حِسَانٌ is the Quranic form illuminated by the source dictionary gloss “chosen women, with no base one among them.”
Joseph's brothers confess لَقَدْ ءَاثَرَكَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا, showing the preference root as God's right elevation of the worthier person.
The Helpers يُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ despite need, enacting the dictionary's good sense of preferring another and ending in success.
وَإِنَّهُۥ لِحُبِّ ٱلْخَيْرِ لَشَدِيدٌ uses ٱلْخَيْر for wealth and makes intense attachment to it part of the human misvaluation.
The foul and the wholesome are not equal even when the foul's abundance impresses, directly correcting a selector who mistakes quantity for good quality.
Givers are told to spend wholesome earnings and not deliberately select the bad portion they themselves would accept only with closed eyes.
وَلَا تَتَبَدَّلُوا۟ ٱلْخَبِيثَ بِٱلطَّيِّبِ forbids exchanging an orphan's sound property for bad property, a concrete wrongful sorting of wealth.
God does not leave the community mixed until He distinguishes the foul from the wholesome, directly staging the section's separation of select from refuse.
God separates foul from wholesome, heaps the foul together, and puts it in hell; the rejected material becomes an accumulated refuse pile.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best are the divinely guided, presenting right selection as discerning and doing the better option.
The Ark bears بَقِيَّةٌ of what the houses of Moses and Aaron left; this sacred remainder carries tranquility and serves as the sign of the chosen king.
وَرَبُّكَ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَآءُ وَيَخْتَارُ reserves creation and choosing to the Lord and denies creatures an independent right of selection.
وَأَنَا ٱخْتَرْتُكَ addresses Moses with the very اختيار form whose dictionary sense the section explains.
وَلَقَدِ ٱخْتَرْنَٰهُمْ عَلَىٰ عِلْمٍ states God's knowledgeable selection of a people over the worlds, a direct use of the dictionary form.
وَإِنَّهُمْ عِندَنَا لَمِنَ ٱلْمُصْطَفَيْنَ ٱلْأَخْيَارِ brings “selected” and “the best” together, matching the section's claim that selection seeks good.
Israel rejects Saul for lacking abundant wealth, but their prophet says God selected him and increased him in knowledge and stature, overturning their worldly criterion of worth.
Noah refuses to drive away the believers whom the chiefs called lowly in 11:27, so the supposed refuse are retained because they will meet their Lord.
وَمَآ أَنَا۠ بِطَارِدِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ is Noah's refusal to discard the followers labeled “the lowest” in 26:111.
Humanity is created فِىٓ أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ, establishing the high-value starting point of the following sorting.
Believers who do right are excepted from the fall to the lowest and receive an unfailing reward, joining goodness to an undiminished remainder.
Earth's adornment is expressly a test of which people are best in deed, so the attractive surface serves divine selection rather than final value.
God will turn that adorned surface into barren soil, supplying the refuse-like end of what 18:7 made temporarily attractive.
Worldly life is rain-mixed vegetation whose full adornment appears secure just before it is made reaped as though it never flourished.
Rain-grown crops vary, yellow, and become debris; the sequence reproduces pasture becoming discard and is offered as a reminder to discerning minds.
The condemned person gathers and repeatedly counts wealth, a concrete attachment to the supposedly chosen worldly portion.
يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُۥٓ أَخْلَدَهُ exposes the mistake of treating accumulated wealth as a source of permanence.
The final home is assigned to those who do not seek elevation or corruption on earth, reversing the instinct to choose worldly height.
God apportions worldly livelihood and raises people in degrees, yet His mercy is better than what they collect, relocating value beyond social rank and accumulation.
After the warning not to be deceived by unbelievers' brief movement through the land, the ayah says what is with God is better for the righteous.
The command turns away from one who turns from remembrance and desires only worldly life, joining exclusive lower desire to rejected guidance.
The Fire's people are told they exhausted their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them there, so their chosen portion leaves humiliation for the present day.
Those not expecting the meeting are pleased and settled with worldly life and heedless of the signs, a full description of the wrong preference.
The Fire becomes their shelter because of what they earned, completing the consequence of the settled worldly choice in 10:7.
Worldly life is adorned for unbelievers who mock believers, but the God-fearing will be above them on resurrection day, reversing apparent rank.
Full recompense comes at resurrection, worldly life is only deceptive enjoyment, and true success is defined by removal from Fire and entry into the Garden.
Worldly life is play and diversion, while faith and reverence preserve the promised rewards rather than consuming people's wealth.
The punishment of the hereafter is أَشَدُّ وَأَبْقَىٰ; it is a direct boundary on treating persistence itself as proof of goodness.
Worldly adornment and wholesome provision are declared lawful gifts for believers and exclusively theirs at resurrection, preventing “worldly” from being treated as intrinsically refuse.
Qarun is told to seek the final home with his gifts without forgetting his legitimate worldly share, a boundary on construing right preference as rejecting every present good.
Those selected to inherit the Book still include a self-wronging group, a moderate boundary on the dictionary ideal that what is chosen contains no low element.
Noah's chiefs label his visibly poor followers أَرَاذِلُنَا; their social sorting mistakes the faithful for human refuse.
Noah is challenged for having ٱلْأَرْذَلُونَ as followers, staging the elite's false identification of low status with low worth.
Pharaoh asks whether he is better than “this contemptible one,” turning worldly kingship and abasement into the very false scale the section corrects.
ثُمَّ رَدَدْنَٰهُ أَسْفَلَ سَٰفِلِينَ supplies the lowest side of the high/low human valuation, before 95:6 preserves the faithful exception.
فَهَلْ تَرَىٰ لَهُم مِّنۢ بَاقِيَةٍ asks whether any remnant of the destroyed people can be seen, the negative edge of the section's valuable remainder.
وَثَمُودَا۟ فَمَآ أَبْقَىٰ states that no one of Thamud was left, contrasting moral remnant with annihilated residue.
The command to persist in prayer and the assurance “We provide for you” give the lived discipline behind 20:131's choice of the Lord's better provision.
Immediately after the magicians choose God as better and more lasting, the criminal's hell is described as a state of neither dying nor living, showing the dreadful side of continued existence.
After the rich man's garden is ruined, true protection belongs to God and He is better in reward and outcome; the collapsed worldly selection leads into 18:45-46's general likeness.
Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth, making the coveted display in 28:79 into discarded ruin.
Those who had desired Qarun's place now recognize God's control of provision and that unbelievers do not prosper, narrating the correction of their choice.
ذَٰلِكَ مَبْلَغُهُم مِّنَ ٱلْعِلْمِ identifies desire for only worldly life in 53:29 as the limit of their knowledge and contrasts it with God's knowledge of guidance.
People whom neither commerce nor sale distracts from remembrance and prayer embody the opposite of the crowd that chose commerce in 62:11.
The believers are commanded not to let wealth or children distract them from remembrance; those who do are named the losers.
Those who forget God are made to forget themselves, sharpening the section's notion that what one discards in choice can turn the chooser into the discarded.
The condemned are told that, because they forgot the meeting of their day, they too are forgotten and made to taste lasting punishment.
The hypocrites forgot God and so He “forgot” them; the reciprocal wording treats willful neglect as exclusion.
مَا قَدَرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ حَقَّ قَدْرِهِۦ uses the measuring root in the sense of valuing God inadequately, the evaluative sense the section points back to from 87:3.
The repeated formula that people did not value God at His true value connects measurement-language to failed spiritual appraisal.
Failure to value God truly is answered by the earth in His grasp and the heavens folded in His hand, exposing the small scale behind worldly misvaluation.
Moses وَٱخْتَارَ مُوسَىٰ قَوْمَهُۥ سَبْعِينَ رَجُلًا, a direct human use of the source dictionary's “choosing” form.
إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا uses “good” for property left behind, exemplifying the section's secondary wealth sense and combining it with what remains at death.
أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ applies “lowest” to extreme old age rather than to a supposedly inferior class of people, a relevant boundary on the refuse metaphor.
The same phrase أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ describes senescence in a resurrection argument, preserving the low-value word while changing its object and moral force.
A destroyed town's people become حَصِيدًا خَٰمِدِينَ, “mown down and extinguished,” a nonlexical parallel to humans made field refuse.
The army is made like eaten straw, another concrete reversal in which the apparently powerful become agricultural residue.
Persistent rejecters are called the worst of creatures and assigned hell, supplying the rejected human side of an explicit best/worst sorting.
Believers who act rightly are called the best of creatures, the selected side opposite 98:6.
The best creatures receive gardens خَٰلِدِينَ فِيهَآ أَبَدًا, joining their goodness to enduring reward.
Unbelievers' works are like ashes violently scattered by wind, a specific image of what cannot be retained from the wrong life.
The good word is a good tree with a firm root, beginning a contrast between stable good and uprooted bad.
The good tree continually gives fruit by its Lord's leave, explaining what beneficial persistence looks like.
The bad word is a bad tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, the discarded counterpart to 14:24-25.
God turns the unbelievers' apparent works into scattered dust, a direct image of selected-looking deeds proving to be refuse.
People do not attain true goodness until they spend from what they love, making correct preference cost the surrender of a favored possession.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts people, a compressed account of abundance becoming the wrongly preferred measure.
The distraction persists until people visit the graves, exposing the temporal limit hidden by accumulation.
The question of what wealth can avail when its owner falls denies accumulated property any power to preserve him.
A person reads abundant provision as divine honor, showing the worldly valuation the following ayat reject.
Restricted provision is read as humiliation, the matching error of confusing measured wealth with human worth.
كَلَّا rejects both readings and redirects value toward honoring the orphan.
وَتُحِبُّونَ ٱلْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا names the excessive love that makes wealth occupy the favored pan.

Solomon's حُبَّ ٱلْخَيْرِ concerns prized horses and remembrance of his Lord; it plausibly exemplifies “good” as valuable property, though the precise relation between that love and remembrance is interpretively disputed.
Feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite love for the food plausibly enacts preferring others over self, though عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ can also be read as love of God.
Those who sell worldly life for the hereafter are summoned to fight, making the rightly directed exchange the inverse of buying this life at the next life's expense.
The warning against seeking the fleeting goods of worldly life adds that abundant gains are with God, correcting both the object and measure of the choice.
Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that both worldly and otherworldly reward are with God, exposing the needless narrowness of choosing only the nearer portion.
People deceived by worldly life turn religion into play and diversion; the command to leave them and remind by the Quran ties the bad preference to its reckoning.
Their portion is only brief enjoyment in the world, followed by return to God and severe punishment, directly measuring the chosen object against its sequel.
After Joseph receives worldly authority, وَلَأَجْرُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ خَيْرٌ preserves the section's hierarchy even within a story of justified earthly success.
People rejoice in worldly life although its enjoyment compared with the hereafter is only slight, while the same ayah locates provision under God's measure.
The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward the enjoyments given to groups of people, a close repeated formulation of 20:131's refusal of worldly display.
The righteous believer is promised a good life and a reward according to the best deeds, showing how 16:96's lasting divine store can include rightly ordered present life.
A brief enjoyment is followed by painful punishment, compressing the passing lower portion and its enduring cost.
The Prophet is commanded to remain with those who call on their Lord and not let his eyes pass beyond them in desire for worldly adornment.
The wealthy man enters his garden wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, explicitly mistaking attractive property for permanence.
He doubts the Hour yet expects an even better return if restored to his Lord, showing the wrong chooser also misappropriating the word “better.”
His produce is encompassed and he wrings his hands over what he spent while the garden lies collapsed, turning the selected display into waste.
The question about those greatest in loss introduces a sorting whose rejected side does not recognize itself.
Their striving is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well, exactly portraying refuse mistakenly selected as good work.
وَٱلْبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ خَيْرٌ repeats the union of remaining good and superior value, while God increases the guided in guidance.
A person who meets God's good promise is contrasted with one merely given worldly enjoyment and then brought for judgment, continuing 28:60's comparison as two human outcomes.
كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُۥ gives the absolute boundary between everything perishing and God alone remaining.
The repeated command not to let worldly life deceive warns that present appearance can corrupt the choice made for the coming day.
God's promise is true, so worldly life must not deceive; the same formula directly pits deceptive nearness against promised reality.
Silver and gold adornment are declared no more than worldly enjoyment, while the hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-fearing.
After worldly vegetation becomes debris in 57:20, the command to race toward forgiveness and a vast garden identifies what should be actively selected.
Noah refuses to say that those whom elite eyes despise will receive no good from God, directly overturning the classification of poor believers as refuse.
Shuayb commands full measure and weight with justice and forbids diminishing people's goods, establishing the clean dealing whose divine remainder is better in 11:86.
Noah answers the charge about lowly followers by denying knowledge of their deeds, refusing the chiefs' superficial basis for sorting them.
Their account belongs only to the Lord, relocating judgment of the supposed human refuse to the one who knows their worth.
People may dislike what is good for them and love what is bad for them; divine knowledge therefore corrects desire as a sufficient rule of selection.
Charity ruined by reproach and display becomes dust on a smooth rock swept bare by rain, a deed chosen for appearance turning into residue with no yield.
Sincere spending is a high garden whose rain multiplies its produce, the fruitful counterpart to 2:264's stripped rock.
A life of a thousand years would still not remove the covetous person from punishment, exposing mere longevity as counterfeit permanence.
A believing slave is better than an admired polytheist, correcting a chooser who confuses social station or attraction with worth.
God makes usury waste away and causes charities to grow, distinguishing wealth that looks productive from clean giving that truly increases.
Captives are told that good known in their hearts can bring them something better than what was taken, placing superior replacement beyond seized property.
The king says of Joseph, أَسْتَخْلِصْهُ لِنَفْسِى, a concrete act of selecting and reserving someone for oneself like the source dictionary's “setting apart” sense.
وَٱصْطَنَعْتُكَ لِنَفْسِى addresses Moses as one formed and set apart for God, a nonlexical enactment of reserving a chosen person to oneself.
The people build monumental structures as though they might live forever, another explicit attempt to extract permanence from worldly possession.
Solomon rejects the envoys' gift because what God has given him is better than what they offer; their delight in the gift reveals the lesser valuation.
Usury given to increase through people's wealth does not increase with God, while alms seeking God's face are the true multipliers.
People infer immunity from punishment from greater wealth and children, making abundance their false proof of chosen status.
God expands and restricts provision, but most people do not know; possession therefore cannot bear the value assigned to it in 34:35.
Neither wealth nor children bring people near to God; faith and right action instead receive multiplied reward and secure chambers.
The command to follow the best of what the Lord has sent down makes discernment of the best an urgent act before punishment arrives.
The owners of the garden are made a test when they swear to harvest it in the morning, beginning a scene in which ownership and selection are morally exposed.
They make no exception for God's will, marking the self-enclosed claim beneath their confidence in the crop.
The garden becomes like a dark, harvested field overnight, turning the expected choice produce into unusable residue.
The owners whisper that no poor person is to enter the garden, revealing that their intended harvest excludes rather than selflessly prefers the needy.
They go out convinced of their power to withhold, the wrong preference immediately before discovering the field's ruin.
On seeing the garden they first think they have lost the way, because the selected property is no longer recognizable.
They then confess that they are deprived, reversing their plan to deprive the poor.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with one better than it, turning loss into a newly corrected request for the better portion.
The passage concludes that worldly punishment is like this but the punishment of the hereafter is greater, measuring the ruined crop against the lasting consequence.
The weighing on that day is true, and those whose scales are heavy are the successful, literally staging one pan and its selected outcome.
Those whose scales are light have lost themselves through wronging the signs, the discarded side of the same weighing.
Heavy scales identify the successful, repeating the selection-by-weight that the section evokes with its two pans.
Light scales identify those who lose themselves and remain in hell, completing the opposed result.
A person with heavy scales begins the surah's compact two-pan sorting.
A pleasing life is the result assigned to the heavy scales.
Light scales introduce the rejected side of the same valuation.
The abyss becomes the light-scaled person's home, completing the choice's terminal contrast.
Full measure and straight weighing are called better and best in outcome, joining honest valuation to the comparative good.
Whatever good people send ahead for themselves will be found with God, so present goods are retained by being transferred toward Him.
